sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Ohio, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Tuesday, October 27Passed

Your application must reach your county board of elections by the close of business on the seventh day before the election: Tuesday, October 27, 2026. (Franklin County, for one, keeps its office open until 8:30 p.m. that day.) Ohio has no online request form; the law allows only mail or delivery in person. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must reach your county board of elections by the close of the polls, 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A postmark is not enough: a law that took effect March 20, 2026 ended the old four-day grace period for mailed ballots. A ballot that arrives late is not counted. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Sunday, November 1, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ohio’s own page on voting by mail

At school away from home, in Ohio or in another state? What Ohio says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. State law lets any qualified voter ask for an absentee ballot, and county boards of elections tell voters they may vote absentee "without providing a reason". (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • By mail. Fill out the Secretary of State's absentee ballot application (form 11-A), sign it, and mail it to the board of elections in the county where you are registered. You must write it yourself: the law says an application is not valid if someone else filled in any part of it. County boards post the form too; Franklin County's copy is linked here. Open it (the law)
  • In person. Hand the signed application in at your county board of elections office, or put it in the board's secure drop box outside its office. (official page)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it to your county board of elections in the return envelope it came with. It must arrive by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, so mail it well ahead. (the law)
  • Drop box. Each county board may have one secure drop box, outside its own office only. It is open around the clock from the day after registration closed until 7:30 p.m. on Election Day, and it is watched by video. (the law)
  • In person. Hand it in at your county board of elections office. Only you or certain close relatives may return it for you: your spouse, parent, parent-in-law, grandparent, brother, sister, child, stepparent, stepchild, adoptive parent or adopted child, uncle, aunt, nephew or niece. No one else may carry it, and it may not be taken to a polling place. (the law)

What the envelope needs

No witness is needed. On the application, and again on the envelope that holds your ballot, give one of these: your Ohio driver's license or state ID card number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number, or put a copy of your photo ID in the return envelope. The application also needs your name, signature, registered address and date of birth. Sign the envelope's statement yourself. (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Ohio’s own site

Ballot tracking is offered by your county board of elections. Franklin County's tracker is linked here; other counties link theirs from their own websites. We could not read the Secretary of State's own tracking page (its website did not answer our request). (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Tuesday, October 6, 2026 to Sunday, November 1, 2026.

You can vote early in person at your county board of elections (or the one early-voting site it names) from the day after registration closed through 5 p.m. on the Sunday before the election: Tuesday, October 6 through Sunday, November 1, 2026. Bring photo ID. Hours differ by day; check your county board's schedule (in Franklin County the last day, Sunday, November 1, runs 1 to 5 p.m.). (the law)

Students

At school in Ohio, away from home

We could not read the Secretary of State's pages (its website did not answer our request), so we could not see whether it speaks to students separately. The state's residence law says your home for voting is the place where you live and mean to return whenever you are away. You do not lose that home by going to another Ohio county for a while, and you do not gain a new home in a county where you stay only for a while without meaning to make it your permanent home. You can ask for an absentee ballot from the county where you are registered and give a different mailing address on the application, such as your school address. (the law)

At school in another state, with Ohio as home

The state's pages that we could read do not speak to students separately. Ohio's residence law says you do not lose your Ohio home by going to another state for a while if you mean to return. You do lose it if you move to another state meaning to make it your home, or if you vote in another state; and, apart from people serving the U.S. government or living abroad, you lose it after living outside Ohio for four years in a row even if you mean to come back. A voter who keeps Ohio as home can ask for an absentee ballot and give an out-of-state mailing address on the application. (the law)

Military and overseas

Military and overseas voters use the Federal Post Card Application to register and ask for a ballot; it must reach the county board by Tuesday, October 27, 2026. You can ask to get your ballot by mail, email or fax. State law counts a mailed ballot whose envelope was signed by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day if it reaches the board by Saturday, November 7, 2026 (four days after the election); the Federal Voting Assistance Program's guide asks for a postmark by Monday, November 2, to be safe. One dropped off in person must arrive by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. Overseas voters can track their ballot on the Secretary of State's military and overseas portal (https://usoav.ohiosos.gov/UOCAVA_vr__Login.aspx). If your ballot has not come, you can use the Federal Write-In Absentee Ballot. (federal guide)

Ohio in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • New for 2026: a mailed absentee ballot must now ARRIVE by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day. In earlier years Ohio counted ballots postmarked the day before and received a few days late; that is no longer so (except for military and overseas voters).
  • If you asked for an absentee ballot and have not sent it back, you can still vote early in person at your board of elections. On Election Day at your polling place you would be given a provisional ballot.
  • The Secretary of State's website (ohiosos.gov) did not answer our requests on October 21, 2026, so the rules above come from the Ohio Revised Code, the Federal Voting Assistance Program and Franklin County's Board of Elections. Early-voting hours and the 8:30 p.m. office hours on October 27 are Franklin County's; your county board can confirm its own.
  • Polls on Election Day are open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.
Where this comes from: 8 pages of Ohio’s election office, its laws and the federal guide
  1. Ohio Revised Code 3509.03, Application for absent voter's ballot (effective April 9, 2025), Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  2. Ohio Revised Code 3509.05, Returning absent voter's ballots (effective March 20, 2026, Senate Bill 293), Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  3. Ohio Revised Code 3509.051, Casting absent voter's ballots in person, Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  4. Ohio Revised Code 3503.02, Residence of voters, Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  5. Ohio Revised Code 3511.11, Uniformed services or overseas absent voter's ballots, Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)
  6. Voting Assistance Guide: Ohio (updated October 5, 2026), Federal Voting Assistance Program (federal guide; read October 21, 2026)
  7. Absentee and Early Voting, Franklin County Board of Elections (official page; read October 21, 2026)
  8. Ohio Revised Code 3501.32, Hours polls open, Ohio Legislative Service Commission (the law; read October 21, 2026)

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: Ohio’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.
